If [the text] were altered, nothing could remain complete without regret; the only reason this [version] stands out above the rest is that it preserves the original intent of the Ishinpo.
Among the various officials of the Song who fixed and edited it, their personal tastes often led to repeated changes in the wording and phrasing.
Scholars of later ages who revised it also did the same; and so the text has already undergone much alteration.
It has been examined quite broadly, and among those who preserve its original form, it is especially esteemed by specialists in medical arts.
As for the lost portions, it is not known how many hundred sections there were, but the Wang family's Waitai Biyao (Arcane Essentials from the Imperial Library) drew upon them.
Now there remain only a few extant family versions, and checking against the bibliographic treatises of the Sui and Tang dynasties,
it is recorded that from the Six Dynasties down through the Tang, the writings of our country's medical arts have survived here.
[Some uncertain text] — recorded in the fifth month of the year hinoto-no-ushi, and now, in the third month of the year kanoe-tatsu, because of this,
passages marked in vermillion ink are those I personally selected while searching through and examining the list of names and the table of contents here.
Those transcribed in blue ink are the annotations made by Master Katsurayama.
My friend Mr. Shima made a shadow-copy for me, following its marginal glosses, and I then
borrowed the thirty fascicles of the Ishinpo by Tanba no Yasuyori from the Taki family, and undertook this compilation and revision.

Yasuyori compiled this book, drawing on more than a hundred sources, all texts of the Six Dynasties and Tang periods. Moreover, there are dozens of works not recorded in the bibliographic treatises and not listed in the Wang family's catalogue. As for the texts that survive today, their format and wording differ considerably. Note the following:

Since ancient times our court's envoys sent to communicate with Tang China, and the students who studied abroad there, followed one another without interruption for more than two hundred years. The books and records they brought back were, at the time, directly obtained transcriptions kept in the palace storehouses and by court scholars — not works that passed through the hands of artisans and merchants as happened under the Hu and Song dynasties. Yasuyori mainly made use of these, and so, although this text preserves the old form of the original books, it differs somewhat from versions that survive elsewhere. Let me cite one or two examples as proof.

Where it quotes the Qianjin fang, there are passages concerning compounding medicines with specific timing, giving ten prescriptions and three treasures, as well as ancient physicians first seeking a cure for illness before all else — yet the various extant editions of this text have repeatedly been cut and abridged. Comparing them with the authentic original, the Qianjin fang here is fully preserved intact. This chapter, [as found in] the red-sheathed hall's original Qianjin fang, survives only in fragments, though many copies are kept in Zan Province.

As for the transcribed copies that have portions missing, there is also the Soshu text, which according to the general catalogue is considered to be based on Su Jing's Bencao. Its sequence of sections and the enumeration of items correspond with the Zhenglei materia medica. The phrasing retains the character of the Tang period, preserving much that is otherwise lost, of value for elementary study.

For example, characters such as "centipede" written as "Wu Ban" (呉班), or "cat" written for "numbness and pain," and the like; or "tiger" written as "white beast," and "ye" written as "qi" — all such instances can be found. Is this not a treasure to be prized and valued? Hence I have, apart from technical matters, noted here as a kind of marginal secret record my discussion of this book.

As for the lower portion of this work, discussion of it does not go back further than the near-ancient period. The details are recorded in the postface by Master Yōkei, which states that in the Eichō era there was a gap, [and that] the white [text] of Hakuraku-tō (the Yoroku-fuji lineage?) Lord So, after extensive search, could never be recovered, and it was said to have long since been lost.

The Ninna-ji temple's register notes it as secret, so that no one could see it; later, in the year of Boat (gai), it was once again sought as a secret text.

In the year of the Tiger [it was] respectfully retired/stored below.

In the bibliographic catalogue of our court, in the Eikyō era, the year of Kinoto-Hitsuji, the Shogun Minamoto no Yoshinori ordered the Great Scholar Kiyohara no Naritada to compile and record it. It came to be known as the Ninna-ji Temple Catalogue; among its entries listed as "scattered and lost" is this one.

(Top margin: brief character glosses, largely fragmentary — explanations of terms such as "bamboo hat," "covering," "garment," "quiver," and "heaven," apparently annotating vocabulary used in the main text. The precise wording is too fragmentary to render with confidence.)

(Main text — continuing the classical discussion, drawn from the tradition of the Huangdi Neijing, of how geography and climate in each of the four directions give rise to different diseases and require different treatments:)

...[The people of the West] dwell on high ground where wind is strong and the soil is hard. They do not wear woven cloth but coarse garments and mats; being well fed and fat, pathogenic influences cannot easily harm their outer form, so their diseases arise from within. Their treatment should employ potent (toxic) medicines.
[This section comes from the "West" passage.]

The North is the region that Heaven and Earth close up and store away. Its land consists of high hills; the wind is cold and the ice freezes solid. Its people delight in open country and live on milk and meat; the cold lodges within them and gives rise to illness. Their treatment should employ moxibustion and cautery.
[This section comes from the "North" passage.]

The South is the place that Heaven and Earth nourish and cause to grow, the region where yang qi is most abundant. Its land is low-lying and damp, with water...

(Left page — colophon:)

I sought to have this book printed and circulated throughout the realm; it had long been kept within [our family], yet remained unrevealed to the world. Now, though I am but a humble and unworthy physician, I have been able with ease to obtain and preserve this book — truly this may be called a great and fortunate blessing. I record this to show to my descendants.

Bunsei 3rd year, 5th month (Satsuki),
Fukuyama Domain,
Izawa Nobuyoshi.

[The place where] mists and dews gather; its people are fond of sour flavors and eat preserved/fermented foods, and so the people have tight-grained [skin] and a reddish complexion. Their diseases are spasms and numbness (痺), and the proper treatment is fine needling — hence the nine needles came from the south.

The central region: its land is level and damp, and Heaven [and Earth] give rise there to many kinds of things; the people eat a mixed diet and do not toil much. Hence their diseases are mostly wasting, reversal (jue), cold and heat; the proper treatment is guided exercise and massage (daoyin anqiao) — hence [these] came from the center.

Thus the sage combines [these different methods] in treatment, so that each obtains what suits it; thus treatments differ yet the illness is cured in every case — this is because one has grasped the true nature of the disease and understands the great principles of treatment.

It is also said: "Whoever wishes to diagnose illness must always ask whether [the patient] was once honored and later became base. Even if [the illness] is not caused by invading evil, the disease arises from within —

this is called 'Loss of Nourishment' (tuoying). One who was once wealthy and later became poor is said to have 'Lost Essence' (shijing). [...]

Those who have Lost Essence and suffer 'Loss of Nourishment' have been injured; those who have suffered disgrace and loss of fat have been injured. Some, once poor, later became wealthy and honored —

the hardship they once endured, though it did not harm them through external evil, harmed their spirit; such [emotional] suffering can indeed bring about disease."

It is also said: "When illness first arises in the yin, first treat the yin and afterward treat the yang. When it first arises in the yang,

first treat the yang and afterward treat the yin. In every case, first treat the root."

It is also said: "When one is bold and takes pleasure, yet the will is troubled, disease arises [...] in the vessels; treat it with moxibustion and needling. When one is bold and joyful in will and takes pleasure, disease arises

in the fat/membranes; treat it with calming of worry, fear and fright. When the vessels are blocked and do not communicate, disease arises

in the sinews; treat it with guided exercise (daoyin). When one is content in will and given to brooding, when one is bold and takes pleasure in will,

but the will is embittered, disease arises, manifesting as moaning and crying out; treat it with medicines, with [measures against] distress and fright."

If there is numbness [insensitivity of the flesh], treat it with massage and medicinal liquors.

The text says: illnesses arising from wind, cold, summer-heat, dampness, diet, or sexual excess, which are not disorders of the heart-mind, may be treated with needle and stone.

Decoctions can remove them. But illnesses caused by joy, anger, worry, and brooding that injure the spirit must be treated by reasoning things through, clarifying and settling the patient's temperament, in order to remove them.

When joy, anger, worry, brooding, and desire become overwhelming, one should use needle and medicine together with spiritual counsel (meditation/guidance) to assist the treatment; needle and medicine alone cannot cure it.

[This is what is meant by] "cure it."

It is further said, Bogao stated: "The art of war says, do not meet head-on a force that comes on like a surging drum-roll; do not strike a formation that stands as solid and imposing as a great hall." The method of needling likewise says: do not needle when the heat is blazing hot, do not needle when the sweat is streaming down, do not needle when the pulse is vast and turbulent, and do not needle when the disease and the pulse are working against each other.

The Zhenjiu Jing (Classic of Acupuncture and Moxibustion) says: for children under ten and the elderly over seventy, needling must not be used — only moxibustion and mild, sweet medicines [are permitted].

[One should] break down the great qi, and only afterward settle and calm it with massage.

Thus, when the evil qi is still vigorous, one must not attack it directly; one should wait until it declines.

The Yimen Fang says: the general rule is that in spring and summer it is appropriate to induce sweating by moxibustion.

Generally, when taking decoctions to induce sweating, once the illness responds one should stop; it is not necessary to use up the whole dose.

In general, when inducing sweat, one should let it come on gradually and spread evenly through the body, moistening it all over at once — this is best. However,

when inducing sweat, even if [profuse, one should] not let it stream and drip like pouring rain; instead apply a rubbing powder to the body, and take care not to expose it to wind or cold.

[page] 3

Whenever there is heavy sweating and the pulse becomes surging and large, as in intermittent fever recurring once a day, induce sweating again; once the sweat comes out, the bowels will ease and the condition will resolve.

Administer Cinnamon Twig and Ephedra Decoction:
Ephedra, 4 liang (nodes removed); Cinnamon heart, 2 liang; Licorice, 1 liang (roasted); Apricot kernel, 80 pieces (tips removed).
Boil in 7 sheng of water: first boil the ephedra until it bubbles, skim off the foam, then add the remaining ingredients and boil down to
2.5 sheng. Divide into three doses, spaced about 7–8 li apart [in time]. After taking, keep covered to bring on sweating again; no congee is needed. The rest follows the method for Cinnamon Twig Decoction.

Cinnamon Twig Method:

Whenever, after sweating has been induced, the sweating continues to leak without stopping, and the patient dislikes wind, has difficulty urinating, and the four limbs feel slightly stiff and hard to move,
treat with Cinnamon Twig Decoction plus Aconite:
Cinnamon heart, 3 liang; Licorice, 2 liang (roasted); Fresh ginger, 3 liang;
Jujube, 12 pieces (split).
Cut the ingredients and boil in 7 sheng of water over a low fire, reducing to 3 small sheng; remove the dregs and divide into three warm doses. Once the decoction has been taken,
shortly after, drink 1 sheng of hot rice congee to assist the medicine's effect; keep warmly covered to bring on sweating. If sweating does not occur, take the dose again
as before. If sweating still does not come, [ ] wait about half a day, until by the next morning one notices its effect, then observe the patient.

If the original symptoms remain, take this decoction again; in some cases, up to three doses may be needed before sweating readily occurs.

"Woman's reins" — this is a separate section.

Thus it is relieved: in the case of the Cinnamon Twig and Aconite Decoction, one additional piece of prepared aconite is added to the decoction.

A text says: "In winter one may apply hot compresses or medicinal fomentation" — ( ) if sweating is induced and sweat appears, with sores developing and vomiting-diarrhea in the mouth, [this is improper].

In cases of strangury (淋家), one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, the eyes will stare fixedly and the patient will be unable to sleep.

In cases of nosebleed (衄家), one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, there will be sinking at the forehead.

When there is blockage in the throat with coughing, one must not induce sweating in such a patient.

After a major purgation, if sweating is then induced, this will cause abdominal distension and fullness.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient feels cold, this indicates deficiency; if the patient does not feel cold but has heat, this indicates excess — in such a case one should harmonize the stomach and nourish the qi.

[Marginal notes]
On Running Piglet Qi (奔豚氣)
Running Piglet patients — origin of the disease, as recorded.
If the lips and tongue are somewhat curled and relaxed,
and a sensation rises from below the navel and rushes up to the heart,
this is due to anxious thought and pent-up qi.

[Heading] Cases in which sweating must not be induced:

In cases of recent severe vomiting and purging, or chest bleeding, or self-exhaustion from blood loss, or after an attack of reversed-flow cough, or in women recently injured by childbirth — in all these, [sweating must not be induced].

In cases of coughing with free urination, or if urinary control is lost, one must not induce sweating; if sweat is forced out, reversed-flow cough will result.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient drinks water excessively, panting will surely result; and if cold water is poured over the body, chronic panting will result.

After sweating has been induced, if the patient feels throbbing below the navel, this indicates an impending attack of Running Piglet Qi; it should be treated with Poria, Cinnamon Heart, Licorice, and Jujube (in large dose).

In cases of sores and ulcers on the body, even though there is bodily pain, one must not attack the exterior [with sweating therapy]; if sweat is forced out, it will certainly bring on spasm (tetany).

Qin Jiao Decoction governs it.

The Classic of Difficulties, Chapter 81, states: The pulse has three sections. The upper section corresponds to Heaven and governs [the region] from the head up to the neck, where diseases occur. The middle section corresponds to Man... The lower section corresponds to Earth and governs [the region] from the navel down to the feet, where diseases occur.

Another authority's great method states: In spring, inducing vomiting is appropriate.

For all diseases located in the chest, inducing vomiting is appropriate.

For fullness together with accumulated phlegm, dry coughing, obstruction of the diaphragm, phlegm nodules causing sudden spasms, and for lung abscess with purulent spitting — [this remedy] is also appropriate.

Whenever a decoction is given to induce vomiting, once the illness responds [and symptoms cease], it is not necessary to finish the entire dose. Those who vomit from... and cold damage affecting the chest —
induce vomiting.

For cases where sweating has already stopped and is followed by abdominal distension and fullness, the Decoction of Magnolia Bark, Pinellia, Licorice, and Ginseng governs it.

Another authority's great method states: In autumn, purgation is appropriate.

For patients who feel aversion to cold yet do not wish to draw their clothing closer, do not induce vomiting.

For those whose leg-qi rises and rushes to the heart, vomiting is not appropriate.

For women who have recently given birth, do not induce vomiting.

For all cases of general weakness and emaciation, do not induce vomiting.

Another source states: For all cases of limb coldness and reversal (jue), do not induce vomiting.

For undigested food lodged in the stomach duct, one should induce both vomiting and purgation.

Another source states: For all diseases located above the diaphragm, inducing vomiting is appropriate.

Whenever a decoction is administered as a purgative, once the illness is relieved the treatment should be stopped — the full dose should not be exhausted.

Whenever a patient with grain-jaundice (gu dan) sweats profusely and urgently, purge them.

Whenever a patient has had abdominal fullness for five or six days without a bowel movement,

and after major purgation, six or seven days pass without a bowel movement, with vexation that does not resolve and abdominal pain with fullness — this indicates dry stool [is present, and purgation is needed].

If this continues and there is retained food, one should use a qi-moving decoction to purge it.

Whenever a patient has difficulty urinating, with the bowel alternating between difficult and easy movement, and at times hiccup and fever without thirst,

and who lies hungry with dryness present — this is because there is dry stool, so purgation is appropriate.

Whenever purgation is indicated, Decoction-Superior Pills are used; pain to one side under the ribs with fever indicates cold, and one should use warming medicine to purge it.

In cases of cold with distension and fullness, purge.

One should purge it.

For dysentery with difficulty urinating — jaundice, water disease, and painful urinary dysfunction (lin disease) that develop after sweating and do not resolve, with abdominal fullness or pain —

in all illnesses with loose stool, in all cold-damage disorders with abdominal fullness, stagnation causing fullness, drum-like distension, or water distension with constipation —

whenever there is fullness and pain in the abdomen due to cold, one should purge; if the fullness does not diminish, it is not worth discussing further.

Purge as usual; if the pulse is rapid and slippery, indicating retained food, purging will bring immediate recovery.

On Symptoms of Diseases That Cannot Be Treated, Chapter Two

Whenever excessive sweating has caused the yang to be lost and the patient becomes delirious, purgation must not be given.
(Note: decoction of burnt salt, a variant text.)

Whenever purging would cause spasm (jing),

In a person who is greatly emaciated, with pain coiling around the navel, there must be retained grain-qi; if one purges through both sides (ribs), the qi will surely rush upward—

Whenever a disease presents with abdominal fullness and vomiting of food, purging it will only make it worse.

Whenever a disease still has external symptoms unresolved, it must not be purged.

Whenever a disease causes a desire to vomit, it must not be purged.

Whenever there is cold-limb reversal (jue), purgation must not be given; the same applies to those of deficient constitution.

Whenever a disease presents with hardness and fullness below the heart, it must not be purged.

Whenever a disease presents with panting and fullness of the chest, it must not be purged.

It is also said that in the summer months, purgation should not be given.

[Continuing the decoction instructions:] Add the rhubarb, boil two or three more times, strain, and divide into two doses; the dose should produce two or three bowel movements as the measure of effect.

Rhubarb, four liang (soaked separately overnight); Magnolia bark, two liang (roasted); cut the ingredients, boil in five sheng of water, reducing it to two and a half sheng.

Whenever purgation is appropriate, use this: the Rhubarb and Licorice Decoction formula—

The Medical Gate Formulary says, discussing this: "Whenever a person falls ill, it always arises from the viscera and bowels. The signs of life and death can all be observed [from without]. It is like an echo answering a sound or a shadow following a form — the response never fails. One must examine this carefully so as never to err." Among these, I will set forth the verified signs in the sections that follow.

In general, whether a person is well or ill, if there are red vessels running from above downward across the upper eyelid, threatening to pierce the pupil — one vessel reaching it means death in one lunar month ["yang" cycle]; two vessels reaching it means death within two months ["li" cycle]. If they have not yet reached down, the condition can still be treated.

If a person's breath becomes suddenly full and bloated, swelling again and again without rest, such a person will die within ten days.

[End of section]

If a person's face suddenly shows a red color appearing over both cheeks and cheekbones [toward the temples], together with a red or black color suddenly rising from the forehead downward to the crown, this signals sudden death; black-red [coloring indicates the same].

If a black-red color suddenly appears on the forehead, as large as a finger, and clings there, death will occur in one day's time, reaching up to the crown, turning red.

If a black color suddenly crosses horizontally over the nose and mouth, extending as far as the area of illness on both sides, this is a sign of sudden death.

If on the face a bluish color suddenly appears resembling a hanging broom, this indicates death by hemorrhage/collapse [an official or elder will die].

If on the nose, between the eyebrows and forehead, a color suddenly appears like horse liver — viewed from a distance it looks blue-yellow, but close up it looks black — death will occur within a hundred days.

[Continuing sign of] death within ten days [as noted].

If the complexion suddenly loses its moisture and lustre, looking as if the illness has just begun, the patient will die.

If the face suddenly becomes puffy and swollen, purely white, with no pattern of blood vessels showing, death will come soon, before long.

If the upper part of the pupil shows a white patch the size of half a grain of rice, the patient will die.

If the face suddenly turns bluish-green and both eyes turn black [in an abnormal way], the patient will die.

If the complexion turns black and both eyes turn white or red, the patient will die.

If the face suddenly turns white and the eyes turn black, the patient will die.

If the face suddenly turns red and both eyes turn white, or if the eyes turn bluish-green, the patient will die instantly.

If the eyes suddenly stare and see nothing, the patient will die.

If the patient's body suddenly gives off an unusual foul odor, the patient will die.

If the patient stares fixedly with pupils that do not move and breathing becomes labored and high, the patient will die.

If the patient's body suddenly loses all sensation of pain or itching, the spirit grows dull and careless, yet eating and drinking continue as before, the patient will die.

If the patient suddenly weeps with sorrow, the patient will die.

If the patient suddenly breaks out in a clean, all-over sweat, the patient will die.

If the patient's face is pale bluish-white, the eyes are wide open and sight is lost, or if the face turns red with disturbed skin texture, and the face, eyes, and nose are all without [color/blood] — [text continues, incomplete]

If the outline of the face or the tongue can no longer distinguish the five flavors, it means the qi of all five viscera is exhausted, and death follows at once.

If the patient's mouth gapes open and he only exhales without drawing breath back in, the lung-qi is exhausted; he will die within three days.

If the patient's back aches and the waist feels so heavy that he cannot turn over, the stomach-qi is exhausted; he will die within five days.

If the patient has diarrhea without being aware that he is passing stool, the spleen-qi is exhausted; he will die within twelve days.

If the patient's limbs and nails turn blue-black, and he shouts and curses without ceasing, the sinew-qi is exhausted; he will die within nine days.

If the patient's hair stands stiff like dry hemp, or white sweat pours out unceasingly, the intestinal-qi is exhausted; he will die within six days.

If the patient's face turns pale-green, he only wishes to lie face-down, his eyes cannot see people, and he weeps without producing tears, the liver-qi is exhausted; he will die within eight days.

If the patient's teeth suddenly ache severely, his face turns truly black, the area above the lip turns yellow, his waist feels as though it were broken, and white sweat pours out like flowing water, the kidney-qi is exhausted; he will die within four days.

If both of the patient's eyes show a yellow color, he will recover before long.

If both outer corners of the patient's eyes show a black color appearing, extending as far as the mouth, he will die — of thirteen such cases, three survive.

If the patient's face and both cheeks turn red, he will die within five days.

If the pupils of the patient's eyes suddenly sink inward, he cannot be treated.

If the patient's eyes are crooked and stare fixedly though breath still remains, he cannot be cured.

If a patient rambles and speaks in confused disorder, or is unable to speak at all — incurable.

If a patient's sweat comes out like beads of pearl and does not flow freely — he will die.

Ge's Prescriptions says: if a child's swelling contains a lump-like mass — incurable.

If the face is swollen and ashen-black, it means the liver has failed — incurable.
If the palms are swollen with no natural lines, full and smooth, it means the heart has failed — incurable.

Bian Que's Transmission states: there are six signs of a disease that cannot be cured.

If a patient's mouth smells foul and cannot close again, with breath going out more than coming in — incurable.

If a patient's face loses its vital color and luster, and he cannot eat or drink — he will die in four days.

If a patient's hands and feet have blackened flesh beneath the nails — he will die in eight days.

If a patient's foot and instep are swollen, and both calves are as large as a peck-measure — he will die in ten days.

Chapter Three: Rules for Taking Medicine

The Qianjin Fang (Prescriptions Worth a Thousand Gold in Gold) says: Bian Que stated, "What a person relies upon is the body; what sustains the body is its vital energy (qi). When the body's qi falls out of harmony, this is illness. One who is arrogant and self-indulgent and does not reason according to principle — this is the first incurable case. One who values wealth over his own body — this is the second incurable case. One who cannot regulate his clothing and food properly — this is the third incurable case. One whose yin and yang, together with the qi of the organs, are unsettled — this is the fourth incurable case. One whose body is so wasted that he cannot take medicine — this is the fifth incurable case. One who trusts shamans rather than physicians — this is the sixth incurable case." This is recorded in the Qianjin Fang, scroll thirteen.

Death.

The Materia Medica Classic (Bencao Jing) says: Cangong had a saying — "A patient who refuses to take medicine is one cause of death. Trusting shamans rather than physicians is also a cause of death."

Another text says: Anyone who would practice medicine must thoroughly observe the root of the disease, understand what has caused it, and treat it first through diet. Only if dietary treatment fails to heal should medicine then be prescribed. [To treat] against the nature of the illness is like a reckless general leading troops — such recklessness only brings excess.

One who does not understand the prohibitions of medicine cannot thereby remove disease; both of these matters must be attended to together, for they are vital and essential.

The essential task in relieving suffering lies with medicine, yet one who does not know what food is suitable cannot thereby preserve life.

To manage vexing poisons is the task of medicine; to save lives and rescue the endangered is the task of the physician; the very foundation of keeping the body at peace depends upon this.

In the practice and etiquette [of medicine], causing harm through excess only worsens matters; being overly cautious of medicine while treating illness leads instead to reckless excess.

To neglect this and fail to study it — how truly lamentable!

[page] Thirteen

It is also said that Zhongjing stated: "When one wishes to treat the various diseases, one should first use decoctions to wash and cleanse the five viscera and six bowels, opening and penetrating the pathways of the pulses, guiding yin and yang, sweeping through the interior to break up pathogenic influences. They moisten what is dry and withered, delight people, benefit the skin, and strengthen the qi. Drinking water purifies all things; this is why decoctions are used. If the four limbs have long-standing illness, or wind-cold has settled in,

powders should be used, for they can disperse and expel pathogenic wind-qi, warming the exterior and strengthening what lies within, with steady and unwavering intent, dispersing accumulations.

As for pills, they can gather and harmonize things, acting together — one who can carry this out may be called a superior physician; this is the physician's intention."

Regarding Ying and Wei (nutritive and defensive qi):
